No. 26A500
IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States 
CITY OF BALTIMORE, MARYLAND, et al., 
Applicants,
v.
STATE OF TEXAS, et al.,
Respondents.
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF APPLICATION TO STAY THE JUDGMENT 
OF THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 
FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS 
ANDRÉS CORREA
YAMAN DESAI
LYNN PINKER HURST & SCHWEGMANN
2100 Ross Avenue, Suite 2700
Dallas, TX 75201
ydesai@lynnllp.com
(214) 292-3639
JOSHUA M. SALZMAN
 Counsel of Record
SIMON C. BREWER
ALLYSON R. SCHER
PAUL R.Q. WOLFSON
BRIAN D. NETTER
DEMOCRACY FORWARD FOUNDATION
P.O. Box 34553
Washington, DC 20043
(202) 448-9090
jsalzman@democracyforward.org

i
STATEMENT PURSUANT TO RULE 29.6 
Applicant Centro Legal de la Raza is a California nonprofit corporation with 
its principal place of business in Oakland, California. It has no parent corporation 
and has no publicly held stock.

1
INTRODUCTION
Remarkably, the Solicitor General asks this Court to deny an application for a
stay of a judgment granting universal vacatur of a consequential federal regulation. 
If that inverted state of affairs were not strange enough, it is all the more
extraordinary because the Federal Respondents all but concede that the judgment is 
invalid because the district court lacked jurisdiction. In the face of Applicants’ 
arguments that the Consent Judgment was the product of egregious collusion to 
circumvent the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and issued in the absence of a 
justiciable case-or-controversy, Federal Respondents offer no response or denial. 
Federal Respondents also do not meaningfully dispute that the attacks they now level 
on Applicants’ standing could have been (but were not) raised against PlaintiffRespondent Texas and that the logical implication of their position is that the district 
court should have rejected the Consent Judgment on standing grounds. See U.S. Opp. 
3, 20–22. Indeed, the clearest statement Federal Respondents offer regarding the 
validity of the Consent Judgment is the vague assurance that non-parties other than 
Applicants may be able to successfully collaterally attack it in the future. U.S. Opp. 
4, 21, 23. Yet, Federal Respondents affirmatively oppose any action that would allow 
Efficient Case and Docket Management in Immigration Proceedings, 89 Fed. Reg. 
46742 (May 29, 2024) (the Rule)—their own duly promulgated regulation—to remain 
in force for even a few additional months pending judicial review. 
This unlikely scenario is the consequence of the continued proliferation of 
rulemaking by collusive acquiescence. The Executive Office for Immigration Review

2
(EOIR) could have followed the APA in seeking to withdraw the Rule. Indeed, during 
the first Trump administration, EOIR followed notice-and-comment procedures in 
issuing a rule that reflected its views regarding administrative closure. See Appellate 
Procedures and Decisional Finality in Immigration Proceedings; Administrative 
Closure, 85 Fed. Reg. 81588 (Dec. 16, 2020). Yet here, EOIR instead colluded with 
Texas to secure the Rule’s invalidation. Unless and until this Court firmly indicates 
that federal jurisdiction is not to be misused in this manner, and that Perez v. 
Mortgage Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. 92 (2015), retains vitality, new and increasingly 
audacious collusive settlements will only continue to proliferate.
Respondents insist that the dubious judgment invalidating the Rule should 
nonetheless remain in force because Applicants lack standing to challenge it. But 
Applicants ask nothing more than that the allegations in Texas’s own successful 
complaint be taken as true. The district court’s judgment necessarily reflects a 
judicial finding that increased removals are a predictable consequence of elimination 
of the Rule and that these removals will affect jurisdictions with large immigrant 
populations (like both Texas and the Cities) at sufficient scale that there is no need
to identify specific immigrants who will be removed. Federal Respondents’ belated 
interest in challenging the underpinnings of that determination should not deprive 
Applicants of the ability to rely upon it. It would be profoundly perverse if the federal 
government’s selective assertion of jurisdictional defenses, and the district court’s 
application of a blatant double standard, were sufficient to insulate a collusive 
judgment from review. In any case, Applicants are not merely uninterested

3
bystanders, but rather, face direct and meaningful injuries as a result of a judgment 
that upends many thousands of immigration cases and predictably leads to the 
removal of the Cities’ residents.
Texas also offers assorted other arguments, but none casts doubt on either the 
certworthiness of the issues or the prospect of ultimate reversal. The district court’s 
judgment, which invalidated a duly promulgated regulation in a single day and 
without adversarial process, should be stayed. 
ARGUMENT
I. THIS COURT IS LIKELY TO GRANT CERTIORARI
Respondents never meaningfully engage with the stakes of this case or the
“host of important questions” regarding rulemaking-by-collusive-acquiescence that it 
implicates. Arizona v. City & County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. 763, 766 (2022)
(Roberts, C.J., concurring, joined by Thomas, Alito, & Gorsuch, JJ.). Respondents 
likewise do not and cannot deny that this case would be a particularly compelling 
vehicle for addressing these important issues because it involves a novel and 
particularly egregious innovation in this area: DOJ announced in advance that it 
would not defend the Rule and then colluded with the plaintiff from the moment suit 
was filed. Nor do Respondents identify any respect in which the template established 
here does not allow for rank circumvention of the APA’s rulemaking requirements in 
any case involving a disfavored regulation. And Federal Respondents do not even 
deny that the underlying merits question of whether EOIR’s longstanding practice of 
administrative closure is statutorily authorized is itself worthy of this Court’s review.

4
In the face of these weighty and certworthy questions, Respondents insist that 
a petition for certiorari in this case would be unlikely to succeed because it would 
involve only a factbound question of intervention law that this Court would be 
unlikely to hear. U.S. Opp. 22; Tex. Opp. 15. But as Applicants explained (at 15–17), 
cases involving the collusive settlement of APA claims are unavoidably bound up in 
questions of whether putative intervenors should be allowed to intervene. Thus, the 
Court is unlikely to view the threshold question of whether Applicants have satisfied 
the standards for intervention in a vacuum, divorced from the context in which the 
question arises. Here, given the blatant misuse of federal courts to evade democratic 
processes and the APA, there is at least a reasonable prospect that this Court would 
grant certiorari to correct this abuse. 
Arizona v. Mayorkas is instructive. In opposing the application for stay 
pending certiorari there, the federal government argued that this Court would be 
unlikely to grant certiorari to consider a “factbound decision” denying intervention 
that “does not conflict with any decision of another court of appeals or otherwise 
warrant further review.” Opp. 18, Arizona v. Mayorkas, No. 22A544 (U.S. Dec. 20, 
2022). The federal government further argued that “derivative effects of a federal 
policy on the States’ own governmental activities do not satisfy Article III or the 
standards governing intervention.” Id. at 5. Yet, this Court was undeterred and
construed the application as a petition for certiorari, which it promptly granted. See 
143 S. Ct. 478 (2022). Federal Respondents insist (at 23 & n.*) that the Article III 
objection there was limited to the question of whether the Mayorkas petitioners had

5
Article III standing to seek a stay pending appeal, but regardless, issues related to a 
putative intervenor’s specific interests could nonetheless have complicated the 
Court’s resolution of the case. The clear lesson of Mayorkas is that in the context of 
interventions that are sought to prevent rulemaking by collusive acquiescence, this 
Court takes account of the broader context in evaluating certworthiness.
Texas notes that the San Francisco concurrence did not decide whether 
“litigation acquiescence violate[s] the APA,” Tex. Opp. 13, but Texas itself recently 
told the Court that it does, see Appl. 14. Texas also insists that the lesson of City & 
County of San Francisco is that there are too many threshold issues implicated by 
such cases for the Court to grant certiorari to address this collusive practice. Tex. 
Opp. 13–14, 16. But the concurrence in that case did not suggest that the host of 
important questions identified there should remain forever unresolved. And this case 
provides a cleaner vehicle than San Francisco because there are no concerns 
regarding mootness or Munsingwear vacatur. See 596 U.S. at 766.
Federal Respondents also argue (at 23–24) that the problem of rulemaking by 
collusive acquiescence is best addressed by cabining the authority of courts to grant 
universal vacatur of federal regulations, a measure the Solicitor General recently
urged this Court to take. See Pet. for Cert., Department of Health and Human 
Services v. Texas Medical Ass’n, No. 26-491 (U.S. Oct. 14, 2026) (TMA). There is a 
certain irony to the Solicitor General pointing to the TMA cert petition—which argues 
that the APA does not authorize universal vacatur, the very remedy the district court 
entered (along with an injunction) against the Rule at issue here—as a reason to

6
allow the Consent Judgment to remain in force. TMA (which arises from the Fifth 
Circuit) is also an apt reminder that the federal government is perfectly willing to 
press its remedial arguments in the face of adverse Fifth Circuit precedent when the 
government is not actively seeking judicial invalidation of its own regulations. 
Furthermore, it is speculative at this point whether certiorari will be granted 
in TMA, let alone whether this Court would ultimately adopt the Solicitor General’s 
position on the merits. But even beyond those issues, the Federal Respondents 
overstate the extent to which narrowing the scope of district courts’ remedial 
authority would defuse the issue of collusive rulemaking. Even party-specific relief 
can substantially upend the status quo, especially when, as here, the plaintiff is a 
large State (or a coalition of ideologically aligned States). The important questions 
posed by the federal government’s willingness to collude to invalidate and enjoin its 
own regulations will persist and merit this Court’s attention regardless. 
II. APPLICANTS HAVE ARTICLE III STANDING
A. The Cities have standing
Respondents’ central objection is that the Cities have not proved their injuries.
But the district court assessed futility under the Rule 12(b)(6) standard: “factual 
allegations are assumed true, the pleading is construed liberally.” App. 88a (citing 
United States v. Texas, 181 F.4th 548, 553–54 (5th Cir. 2026)). Texas defended the 
district court’s reliance on that futility framework below, Tex. C.A. Opp. 7, and 
neither respondent disputes it here. Under that standard, courts “must accept as true 
all material allegations . . . and must construe the complaint in favor of the 
[claimant].” Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490, 501 (1975). “[G]eneral factual allegations

7
of injury resulting from the defendant’s conduct may suffice,” because courts 
“presum[e] that general allegations embrace those specific facts that are necessary to 
support the claim.” Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 561 (1992). Yet 
Respondents insist that the Cities identify a specific taxpayer, crime victim, or 
recalendared case. U.S. Opp. 3, 12, 15–16; Tex. Opp. 18, 21. That is a demand for
proof the standard does not require.
The Cities need nothing more than the premise Texas itself pleaded and the 
district court accepted. Texas alleged that vacatur “will necessarily reduce the 
number of cases administratively closed and, therefore, reduce the number of illegal 
aliens permitted to remain.” App. 27a. Respondents call the Cities’ injuries 
speculative because they depend on removals. U.S. Opp. 11–13; Tex. Opp. 17–18. But 
more removals are “the whole point” of the judgment Texas and Federal Respondents
jointly sought. Cf. Diamond Alt. Energy, LLC v. EPA, 606 U.S. 100, 118 (2025) (“[I]f 
invalidating the regulations would change nothing in the market, why are EPA and 
California enforcing and defending the regulations?”). Those removals will cost the 
Cities income-tax revenue from work-authorized residents, App. 53a ¶¶ 12–16; App. 
81a–82a ¶ 9, and the cooperation of crime victims who, without closure, face removal 
while prosecutors still need them, App. 82a ¶ 10; App. 74a ¶ 17; App. 83a ¶ 18. See
Appl. 19–21. If Texas’s premise was enough to support a judgment entered the day 
its complaint was filed, it is enough to support the Cities’ standing to appeal that 
judgment.

8
Nor is Texas differently situated. Every argument Federal Respondents make 
against the Cities’ standing applies equally to Texas. Federal Respondents say the
Rule does not regulate the Cities. U.S. Opp. 11. It does not regulate Texas either. The 
Cities’ injury depends on a “multi-step chain” of decisions by immigration judges and 
DHS. Id. at 2–3. So does Texas’s. The Cities do not identify an individual noncitizen 
who will be removed. Id. at 12. Neither did Texas. Federal Respondents’ principal 
attempt to distinguish Texas—that administrative closure supplies “legal benefits” 
such as “work authorization,” id. at 21—describes the very source of the Cities’ tax 
revenue (and resulting injury). App. 53a ¶¶ 12–14; App. 81a–82a ¶ 9. Nor do the 
Cities seek to keep noncitizens “with valid removal orders” in the country, U.S. Opp. 
21; an administratively closed case has no final removal order to execute. And United 
States v. Texas, on which Federal Respondents rely (at 3, 13), held that States lacked 
standing to challenge federal immigration-enforcement policy notwithstanding the 
costs they alleged. 599 U.S. 670, 680 & n.3 (2023). 
Respondents’ objection that the judgment does not require any closed case to 
be recalendared, U.S. Opp. 3, 12, 18; Tex. Opp. 18, 24, fails twice over. First, 
recalendaring is the predictable and intended consequence of the Consent Judgment. 
The parties sought the judgment precisely because it would “reduce the number of 
cases administratively closed.” App. 27a. Nor do Federal Respondents deny that the 
Consent Judgment spurred recalendaring motions. Indeed, that appears to be 
happening across the country. See, e.g., Catholic Legal Imm. Network, Inc., Updates 
on Administrative Closure and Termination: The State of Play 3 (Sept. 2026)

9
(“[P]ractitioners have reported another wave of motions to recalendar being filed by 
[federal government attorneys] after the [district court’s] decision.”), 
https://perma.cc/74X6-7V4V.
Second, and more fundamentally, the Cities’ injuries do not depend on 
recalendaring. Even if no closed case reopens, the prospective effects are significant. 
Active cases that would have qualified for closure or termination under the Rule will 
instead continue. Those cases belong not only to U visa petitioners but also to asylum 
and TPS applicants, among others, who may work while their cases are pending. See
8 C.F.R. § 274a.12(c)(8), (19). Indeed, Texas’s suit depends on the proposition that 
cases that would otherwise be administratively closed or terminated will now be 
“adjudicated to completion, and [the noncitizens] removed.” App. 25a. Take that 
premise as true, and vacatur will produce more removals nationwide. That will cost 
the Cities tax revenue as their taxpayers are removed, App. 53a ¶¶ 12–16; App. 81a–
82a ¶ 9, and will impair public safety as their crime victims decline to cooperate with 
law enforcement, App. 74a ¶ 17; App. 83a ¶ 18. Texas cannot claim that vacatur will 
remove noncitizens across the country while insisting that none of them will be the 
Cities’ taxpayers or crime victims.
The Cities’ tax injury is precisely the kind that Wyoming v. Oklahoma, 502 
U.S. 437 (1992), recognizes, and Respondents’ efforts to distinguish it as insufficiently 
“direct” fail. U.S. Opp. 13–14; Tex. Opp. 18–19. In Wyoming, the statute regulated 
Oklahoma utilities, not Wyoming. The State’s injury was “direct” even though it arose 
from those purchasers’ decisions, which reduced the coal sales Wyoming taxed. 502

10
U.S. at 447–48. In Diamond, the fuel producers’ standing likewise depended on how 
automakers and consumers would respond if California’s standards were invalidated, 
and the Court drew “commonsense inferences” about that response. 606 U.S. at 116; 
see id. at 117–20. That principle is not confined to markets: “[a]cross contexts,” courts 
may draw such inferences about “third party behavior.” First Choice Women’s Res. 
Ctrs., Inc. v. Davenport, 608 U.S. 174, 189–90 (2026). The chain from vacatur to 
removals to lost tax revenue is no less predictable. Appl. 19–20. Florida v. Mellon, on 
which Federal Respondents rely, is different. There, the loss depended on speculation 
that taxpayers would choose to “withdraw property from the state.” 273 U.S. 12, 17–
18 (1927). Here, the Cities’ taxpayers will be removed through the very process Texas 
sued to set in motion. App. 27a.
Nor is the Cities’ loss the “decline in general tax revenues” that Wyoming
distinguished. U.S. Opp. 14 (quoting 502 U.S. at 448). The Cities allege “a loss of 
specific tax revenues,” 502 U.S. at 448, in the form of municipal income taxes paid by 
work-authorized residents who now face removal. App. 53a ¶¶ 12–16; App. 81a–82a 
¶ 9.
The Cities’ law-enforcement injury is just as concrete. Federal Respondents
say the Cities never allege a resident with a pending U visa petition in closed 
proceedings. U.S. Opp. 15. They do. App. 84a ¶¶ 20–21. Federal Respondents call the 
Cities’ theory “speculation about the unfettered choices made by independent actors.” 
U.S. Opp. 16–17. But as Texas explained, closure is a “well-understood incentive” to 
which third parties will predictably respond. App. 25a. And Federal Respondents’

11
“other mechanisms” are no substitute. U.S. Opp. 16. Administrative closure took a 
case off the “active calendar.” Id. at 5 (quoting Matter of Avetisyan, 25 I&N Dec. 688, 
692 (BIA 2012)). A continuance does not. The case stays “on the active docket,” Tex. 
Opp. 33, and U visa petitioners no longer enjoy a “presumption in favor of a 
continuance,” Matter of L. Ramirez, 30 I&N Dec. 157, 160 (BIA 2026). Deferred action, 
too, leaves the case on the active docket. It does not foreclose removal but makes a 
noncitizen “a lower priority for removal,” 3 USCIS Policy Manual pt. C, ch. 5, § C.7, 
https://perma.cc/L5VT-S4XL (captured Oct. 23, 2026), and it comes, at the earliest,
after a bona fide determination that now takes a median of 15.2 months and that 
USCIS issues 80 percent less often than it did on average in fiscal year 2025. USCIS, 
Number of Form I-918, Petitions for U Nonimmigrant Status, by Fiscal Year, Quarter, 
and Case Status: Fiscal Year 2026, Quarter 3 (2026), https://perma.cc/2BHA-53WB
(captured Oct. 23, 2026); USCIS, Number of Service-wide Forms by Quarter, Form 
Status, and Processing Time: Fiscal Year 2026, Quarter 3 (2026), 
https://perma.cc/GDQ6-BT8P (captured Oct. 23, 2026). Without administrative 
closure, victims who come forward face active removal proceedings while their 
petitions wait. That is what keeps them from coming forward. App. 83a ¶ 18.
B. Centro Legal has standing
As Applicants explained (at 22–25), Centro Legal also suffers an Article III 
injury traceable to the Consent Judgment. By vacating the Rule, the Consent 
Judgment directly impairs the availability of administrative closure—a procedural 
mechanism on which Centro Legal relies in its work—and will trigger contractual 
obligations to represent existing clients in renewed proceedings, at considerable cost

12
to Centro Legal. App. 63a–64a ¶¶ 21–24, 69a ¶ 36. Those “[m]onetary costs are of 
course an injury.” Diamond, 606 U.S. at 111; see also, e.g., Dep’t of Com. v. New York, 
588 U.S. 752, 767 (2019) (holding that States had standing based, in part, on 
anticipated losses of federal funding). 
Respondents’ contrary arguments rest almost entirely on this Court’s decision 
in Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine. That decision does not support their position. 
The Court explained that the plaintiffs—doctors who objected to the FDA’s rules 
regarding mifepristone—lacked “standing to sue simply because others are allowed 
to engage in certain activities.” 602 U.S. at 393. The doctors attempted to rely on a
“speculative” chain of reasoning that “lack[ed] record support” to demonstrate 
downstream financial injuries from the availability of a drug they neither prescribed 
nor used. Id. at 390. In that context, this Court declined to create a unique “doctrine 
of ‘doctor standing’” that would allow physicians to challenge “general public safety 
requirements” merely because those regulations may result in some downstream 
injuries that they could treat. Id. at 391.
Those facts bear little resemblance to the injuries Centro Legal asserts here. 
To start, Centro Legal is not challenging the under-regulation of some third party. 
Rather, it contests the Consent Judgment’s effect on its “core business activities.” 
Alliance, 602 U.S. at 395. As the record demonstrates, Centro Legal uses 
administrative closure in its core business of representing clients, including in its 
business decisions about how many clients to take. See App. 54a–61a ¶¶ 3–14.
Respondents do not, and could not, contest that such representation is Centro Legal’s

13
core business. See, e.g., App. 54a–56a ¶¶ 3–10. As a result, a change to the governing 
legal regime that makes that business more costly and less effective directly harms 
Centro Legal. That is why Centro Legal previously sought and obtained a preliminary 
injunction regarding the 2020 rule restricting administrative closure, see Centro 
Legal de la Raza v. EOIR, 524 F. Supp. 3d 919 (N.D. Cal. 2021), and dismissed its 
case only after the Rule rescinded the 2020 regulations.
The happenstance that Centro Legal’s business activities are pro bono legal 
representation, rather than some for-profit enterprise, makes no difference to the 
standing analysis. For-profit businesses unquestionably have Article III standing to 
contest a regulatory change that would “deprive them of potential clients”—the very 
injury Federal Respondents dismiss, U.S. Opp. 19. In Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 
U.S. 510 (1925), for example, private schools had standing to challenge a state law 
that restricted their client base, “even though parents were the directly regulated 
parties.” Diamond, 606 U.S. at 115. The outcome would have been no different if the 
schools were nonprofit organizations. The fact that the challenged regulation makes 
the organization’s business activities more difficult, and restricts its ability to serve 
clients, constitutes an Article III injury. And to the extent that the Federal 
Respondents suggest (at 18) these injuries are “self-inflict[ed]” because Centro Legal 
has chosen to engage in pro bono immigration representation, that merely reprises 
the argument this Court rejected in FEC v. Cruz, 596 U.S. 289, 296–97 (2022).
Respondents mistakenly suggest (U.S. Opp. 19–20; Tex. Opp. 23) that Centro 
Legal’s injuries are too attenuated to support standing. To the contrary, those injuries

14
are the direct, predictable, and intended consequences of the Consent Judgment. As 
explained above, the parties sought the Consent Judgment precisely because it would 
reduce the availability of administrative closure, and recalendaring is its predictable 
result. Supra pp. 8-9. Recognizing that result requires no speculative chain of 
causation about distant third-party decisions akin to the one rejected in Alliance, but 
instead turns on the same “commonsense inferences” that support the Cities’ 
standing, supra p. 10; see Diamond, 606 U.S. at 116; First Choice, 608 U.S. at 190, 
and that Texas itself insisted upon in demonstrating its own standing. Centro Legal’s 
80 to 100 administratively closed cases are among those that stand to return to active 
dockets. App. 61a–63a. It is therefore entirely predictable that Centro Legal will 
suffer the attendant financial and workload harms. 
At bottom, Respondents ask the Court to endorse a rule of standing that 
imposes uniquely difficult barriers for legal-services providers to demonstrate a 
cognizable injury. But this Court has “repeatedly rejected requests to create special 
standing rules for particular litigants.” Bost v. Ill. State Bd. of Elections, 607 U.S. 71, 
86 (2026) (Barrett, J., concurring in judgment); see also, e.g., Alliance, 602 U.S. at 392 
(rejecting a standing theory that would create different standing rules for different 
professions). For good reason: Article III does not create disfavored classes of 
litigants. Standing is an “unchanging part of the case-or-controversy requirement,” 
Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560, and there is no basis for requiring legal-services providers to 
make a heightened showing of their organizational standing. Far from opening the

15
floodgates to litigation, recognizing Centro Legal’s standing would represent an 
evenhanded application of the neutral rules this Court’s precedents establish.1
III. THE OTHER FACTORS FAVOR A STAY
A. Applicants have a fair prospect of reversal on the merits
For the reasons set forth in our application (at 26–33), there is a fair prospect 
this Court will reverse on the merits. The judgment was entered without jurisdiction, 
enables evasion of the APA’s rulemaking procedures, and does not faithfully apply 
the underlying statutory law. In addition, the Consent Judgment far exceeds the 
scope of any permissible relief. 
Federal Respondents do not meaningfully contest any of these fundamental
flaws with the judgment. Instead, they repeatedly suggest (at 4, 21, 23) that the 
Consent Judgment may be collaterally attacked. That all but concedes that 
Applicants have raised important, meritorious issues that create a fair prospect of 
reversal.
For its part, Texas attempts to defend the Consent Judgment, but each of its 
arguments falls far short. 
1 The Federal Respondents’ citation (at 19) to INS v. Legalization Assistance Project 
of the Los Angeles County Federation of Labor, 510 U.S. 1301 (1993) (O’Connor, J., 
in chambers), is particularly misplaced because that decision concerned the “zone of
interests” test that governs whether a given plaintiff can assert a cause of action
under the APA. Id. at 1305. It is not an Article III case and has little bearing on 
whether Applicants have a constitutionally sufficient stake in this case to intervene 
as defendants.

16
1. Texas does not deny that the parties coordinated this suit to obtain a 
preordained outcome. Nor does it deny that from the moment the complaint was filed, 
“both litigants desire[d] precisely the same result.” Moore v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg 
Bd. of Educ., 402 U.S. 47, 48 (1971) (per curiam). As a result, it fails to identify any
adverse interests the parties possessed at any point in this litigation. Instead, Texas 
offers cursory citations to INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919 (1983), and United States v. 
Windsor, 570 U.S. 744 (2013), for the proposition that the district court possessed 
jurisdiction. Tex. Opp. 28. Neither case involved the kind of rank collusion evident 
here, and each involved adversarial presentation. 
2. Texas next suggests that the APA’s notice-and-comment procedures for 
repealing a rule, 5 U.S.C. § 553(b), are inapplicable because the parties proceeded via 
Consent Judgment. Tex. Opp. 29–31. Texas makes no effort to reconcile this 
argument with its prior positions before this Court. See, e.g., Br. for Pet’rs at 3, 
Arizona v. City & County of San Francisco, No. 20-1775 (U.S. Dec. 13, 2021) (S.F. 
Br.).
In any event, Texas misconstrues Applicants’ argument. The question is not 
whether Section 553 binds a court. Contra Tex. Opp. 29–31. Rather, the question is 
whether Federal Respondents evaded their own legal obligations by engaging in 
“rulemaking-by-collusive-acquiescence.” City & County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. at 
766 (Roberts, C.J., concurring). Neither respondent disputes that, if DOJ wished to 
repeal a duly promulgated regulation, it would need to follow notice-and-comment 
procedures. And Texas does not dispute that an agency could not revoke a rule

17
without following notice and comment merely by confessing some newfound defect. 
Tex. Opp. 30. In light of that, it is hard to see why agencies should be able to leverage 
consent judgments in friendly litigation to evade those strictures. After all, this Court 
frequently has observed that “a government official cannot do indirectly what she is 
barred from doing directly.” Nat’l Rifle Ass’n of Am. v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175, 190 (2024). 
That is precisely what DOJ has accomplished here by substituting manufactured 
litigation for proper rulemaking procedures. 
3. Texas’s explanation (at 32–34) of why the Consent Judgment correctly 
construes the INA largely elides the operative statutory text. It offers no meaningful 
account of DOJ’s authority to adopt rules governing its own agency proceedings, 8 
U.S.C. § 1103(g)(2), nor of the Homeland Security Act of 2002’s carry-forward of 
preexisting authorities and functions, Pub. L. No. 107-296, § 1102, 116 Stat. 2135, 
2274. See Appl. 28–30. And Texas now retreats from the sole authority cited to and 
relied upon by the district court, Hernandez-Serrano v. Barr, 981 F.3d 459 (6th Cir. 
2020); see App. 45a–46a, 49a. Texas belatedly acknowledges (at 33) that “HernandezSerrano does not resolve this case,” because there, the Sixth Circuit held only that an 
earlier regulation, which let immigration judges take actions necessary for the 
“disposition” of a case, did not itself authorize administrative closure. 981 F.3d at 
463–64. It did not decide whether the INA permits the Attorney General to authorize 
administrative closure by regulation, as the Rule does. But see App. 49a (district 
court’s final judgment citing only to Hernandez-Serrano for the proposition that “no

18
statute authorizes immigration judges to indefinitely administratively close or 
suspend adjudication of a case before them”).
To the extent Texas engages with the Rule’s legality, its argument is largely 
ipse dixit. That, again, illustrates the fundamental problem with this suit: the district 
court never received adversarial briefing on the key merits questions before entering 
judgment, so it had no opportunity to weigh these unsupported assertions against 
countervailing views. This Court is likely to conclude, as several circuits previously
recognized, that “[a]dministrative closure is a procedural device that temporarily 
takes a removal case off of an immigration judge’s calendar.” Meza Morales v. Barr, 
973 F.3d 656, 664 (7th Cir. 2020). As a result, the Rule is a proper exercise of the 
Attorney General’s authority to establish procedures governing immigration courts. 
4. Finally, Texas makes essentially no effort to defend the injunction’s patent
overbreadth. Its opposition does not dispute (at 34–36) that the regulation is 
severable, and it cannot explain why it suffers any injury either from unchallenged 
portions of the Rule or from hypothetical future rulemakings regarding 
administrative closure. Instead, Texas half-heartedly suggests (at 35) that Applicants 
have no interest in the Rule’s other provisions. Centro Legal clearly identified its 
interest in termination as well as administrative closure, App. 63a, and it certainly 
has a more concrete interest in immigration-court procedures than Texas does. In any 
event, severability is a remedial inquiry that does not turn on “the interests of the 
parties.” Levin v. Com. Energy, Inc., 560 U.S. 413, 427 (2010) (quoting Califano v. 
Westcott, 443 U.S. 76, 96 n.2 (1979) (Powell, J., concurring in part and dissenting in

19
part)). At an absolute minimum, Applicants are likely to demonstrate that the 
Consent Judgment’s overbroad relief must be narrowed. Cf. Trump v. CASA, Inc., 606 
U.S. 831, 841 (2025).
B. The equities favor a stay
Respondents’ irreparable-harm arguments largely repackage their standing 
arguments. U.S. Opp. 24–25; Tex. Opp. 36–38. There is no suggestion that Applicants’ 
harms, though cognizable, can be redressed at the conclusion of the litigation. The 
same harms that establish standing also establish irreparable injury.
The remaining factors are not close. The Rule was adopted through notice and 
comment and can be repealed only the same way. Mortg. Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. at
101. EOIR did not do so. Instead, it obtained vacatur, and a permanent injunction 
binding future administrations, through a Consent Judgment entered within hours 
of the complaint. App. 1a, 44a–50a. Texas argues that a stay is unwarranted because 
DOJ has not sought one. Tex. Opp. 40. That is the problem, not the answer. The desire 
of federal officials to circumvent the APA’s rulemaking provisions does not detract 
from the public’s interest in seeing validly enacted regulations continue in force until 
they are validly repealed. Texas once agreed: it told this Court that the federal 
government must “respect [a] duly enacted Rule until it repeals it through noticeand-comment rulemaking.” Appl. 28 (quoting S.F. Br. 3).
Texas, meanwhile, will suffer little from a stay. It lived with the Rule for two 
years and sued only after EOIR announced it would no longer defend it. App. 1a, 
107a. Nor would Federal Respondents be harmed by adhering to the Rule until it is

20
validly rescinded. EOIR itself has instructed its adjudicators that the Rule remains 
binding until then. App. 107a.
CONCLUSION
The Court should stay the Consent Judgment pending the Fifth Circuit’s 
disposition of Applicants’ appeal and, if necessary, the disposition of a timely petition 
for a writ of certiorari.
